summary: NeuroNexus Martian Map is a web console that helps a future Mars explorer decide where to walk, how long it takes and what it costs. It layers NASA MOLA topography, HiRISE and CTX terrain, MSL/RAD radiation, Ames MGCM dust and THEMIS thermal data with USGS geology and Curiosity and Perseverance traverses. A deterministic planner generates multi-objective routes and reports a planning-limit status for each one (within limits, review required, exceeds limit), never claimed as "100% safe". Every value carries a source tag and its uncertainty, and the terrain model is validated against real rover drives at Gale and Jezero. Missing data shows as unavailable instead of being invented. Gemini and other fallback providers only explain structured results; it never creates routes or changes a number. Runs in any browser, on laptop, desktop, iPad, tablet and phone.
details:
NeuroNexus

THE QUESTION BEHIND EVERY MARSWALK

Before an astronaut steps onto Mars, one question decides everything: is it safe to walk here right now, and what science can I do along the way? Today the answers live in separate datasets, separate tools and separate papers. NeuroNexus: Know the Ground Before You Walk It puts them on one map, so the map itself becomes the decision.

IMAGE (hero screenshot: the three synchronized maps)

WHAT WE BUILT

- Three maps that move together: a 2D map with all 2,052 USGS/IAU named Martian features, an interactive 3D globe and the USGS geologic map. Click one and the other two follow.

- AI Route Designer: a deterministic multi-objective search over a terrain ladder (HiRISE 1 m, then CTX, then MOLA) that returns candidate routes for lowest distance, EVA time, terrain burden, science value and terrain risk.

- MARSWALK EVA planner: pick a site, up to five stops and an EVA duration. The console returns a decision (WITHIN PLANNING LIMITS, REVIEW REQUIRED or EXCEEDS PLANNING LIMIT), a turnaround point, pace and metabolic estimate, elevation and slope profile, dose screening and a status-by-sol ribbon.

- Exports an astronaut can carry: EVA brief (JSON), route GeoJSON and CSV, a printable brief, route comparison and validation reports.

IMAGE (MARSWALK EVA planner console)

HOW IT ANSWERS THE CHALLENGE: LAYERS OF DECISIONS, NOT LAYERS OF DATA

Each layer answers one question an explorer would ask before going outside.

- Terrain (MOLA, CTX, HiRISE): can I physically get there, and how steep is the ground?

- Radiation (MSL/RAD dose rates): what dose does this plan screen at?

- Atmosphere (Ames MGCM dust by sol): how does dust change the plan over time?

- Thermal (THEMIS): what is the ground temperature history?

- Geology (USGS SIM 3292): what is worth studying along the way?

- Ground truth (Curiosity and Perseverance): does the model match what real rovers felt?

IMAGE (layer panel with radiation, dust and terrain)

WHY THE SHORTEST ROUTE IS A TRAP

On our Gale to Escalante benchmark, the lowest-distance route is 1,464.72 km with 31,332 m of climb. A candidate only 480 m longer cuts the climb to 22,597 m. A single shortest-path answer hides that trade-off. Our Pareto set shows it, so the explorer negotiates between distance, effort, risk and science instead of accepting one number.

IMAGE (route comparison / Pareto view)

DUST AND TIME: THE SAME WALK CAN BECOME UNSAFE

Across Mars Year 34, the planner records 668 sols of status outcomes as dust optical depth changes: 0 WITHIN PLANNING LIMITS, 570 REVIEW REQUIRED, 98 EXCEEDS PLANNING LIMIT. Scrub the sol slider to the 2018 global dust storm (sol 400, tau 4.62) and the same Gale plan flips to EXCEEDS PLANNING LIMIT.

(sol slider during the 2018 dust storm)

VALIDATED AGAINST REAL ROVERS

We tested our terrain model against end-of-drive tilt data from Curiosity and Perseverance. Coarse 463 m MOLA underestimates the p90 steep ground by 1.79x at Gale and 2.35x at Jezero. A 1 m HiRISE surface evaluated at a 3 m rover-scale baseline reproduces felt tilt at 0.99x (Gale) and 0.92x (Jezero). Gale was our development site; Jezero ran the same code with no re-tuning. Every metric reports n, an estimate and a 95% bootstrap interval, and plans are byte-identical when re-run.

IMAGE (rover validation chart from landing page)

HONEST BY DESIGN

- Every layer is labeled OBSERVED, MODELED, DERIVED, COMPUTED, SIMULATED or UNAVAILABLE. Nothing is called NASA-certified safe, and planning limits are not safety limits.

- Known limits are shown in the interface: a 7.3 m HiRISE/CTX seam bias (seam pixels are flagged), the 215-day lag of the archived RAD data, and thermal data shown as unavailable when no reference is in range.

- The dose value is a screening estimate from archived RAD dose rates at Gale, not a radiation-transport prediction. Sensitivity bars show which planning choices drive the result.

- Every value carries a source tag that resolves to a 76-entry source ledger. Sources we cataloged but did not ingest, such as MCS and CRISM, are labeled that way.

IMAGE (source tags / provenance panel)

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

- In the app: Mars Intelligence uses the Google Gemini API through 27 read-only tools to explain structured results. It never creates route geometry or changes a number, and its output is labeled AI INTERPRETATION, never a NASA observation. If Gemini fails, fallback providers (Groq, Mistral, NVIDIA, Cohere, OpenRouter, GitHub Models) are tried in order.

- Peer review: ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude all reviewed our architecture, code, science claims and wording. ChatGPT and Claude helped solidify the architecture, Grok added further reviews and Gemini helped with asset generation.

- Code and delivery: ChatGPT and Claude helped with coding, with GitHub Copilot contributing a few commits. Claude, using MCP servers, connectors, plugins and a browser extension, helped us develop, deploy and submit, and helped edit our videos.

- All route geometry, slopes, doses and statuses come from deterministic code on NASA and USGS data, not from a language model. The team made every final decision.

IMAGE (Mars Intelligence panel; label any SI-generated image)

BUILT WITH

React 19, Vite, Leaflet, ArcGIS Maps SDK and Three.js on the front end; FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio and xarray on the back end. 270 backend tests, 120 frontend tests and 71 device checks across desktop, iPad, iPhone and Android emulation.

WHAT WE WOULD BUILD NEXT

Ingest MRO MCS profiles as a second atmospheric source, add an anomaly flag on the RAD time series, run field tests on real phones and tablets, and extend the terrain ladder to more sites.
